guide.title: Read these before you start.
guide.lead: We turn the most common decisions into short notes: how to choose a service, estimate usage and keep the bill predictable.
guide.cta: Still have questions? Talk to an engineer
guide.post.1.title: Sizing your first service
guide.post.1.excerpt: CPU, memory, bandwidth and disk are not a contest. Define the shape of the workload first, then choose the configuration.
guide.post.1.body:
The most common sizing mistake is buying for a future you have not defined. A better approach is to write down what the machine will run for the next three months: a static site, an API service, or a batch of scheduled jobs.

For a static site or a light API, two cores and 4 GB is usually enough. The bottleneck tends to be the network, not the CPU. For a database or a build node, memory and disk IO matter more than core count.

Estimate bandwidth from the peak, then leave 30% headroom. Do not derive bandwidth from monthly traffic; for most workloads those two numbers are not linear.

Finally, buy one size smaller. The value of cloud is that you can upgrade, not that you can predict everything up front. Watch real load for a week, then decide.
guide.post.2.title: Keeping a service bill predictable
guide.post.2.excerpt: Runaway bills rarely come from a high unit price. They come from a few dimensions that grow quietly with no owner.
guide.post.2.body:
Split the bill into four categories: fixed resources, elastic resources, traffic and storage. Fixed resources can be reserved. Elastic resources need quotas and alerts. Traffic is reduced through architecture. Storage needs a lifecycle policy.

Set a budget ceiling for each category and wire it into monitoring. A budget is not a finance artifact; it is a technical decision that forces you to choose which growth is worth it.

Spend ten minutes a week on anomalies. Any dimension that grows more than 20% for three weeks usually has a concrete cause: a snapshot nobody cleaned up, a detour in the origin path, or a test machine left running.

A predictable bill is not saved. It is designed.
guide.post.3.title: Cross-border access is slow. What first?
guide.post.3.excerpt: Before adding machines, separate first-byte latency, low throughput and packet loss. Each has a different fix.
guide.post.3.body:
Measure time to first byte. If the TCP handshake alone takes hundreds of milliseconds, the problem is routing and distance. More bandwidth will not help. Local peering or a dedicated line is the fix.

If the first byte is fine but downloads are slow, check congestion windows and packet loss. Random loss on a cross-border path collapses throughput. The answer is retransmission strategy, not simply more capacity.

If only one region is slow, inspect DNS resolution first. Many “network problems” are actually traffic resolved to the wrong edge node.

Only then consider adding machines. With infrastructure, measure before you move.
